sentences.text: Ultrastenos was a small crocodilian that measured upwards of 1.5 meters in length and possessed a flattened, short snout.
Its external nostrils were positioned very close to the tip of the snout, giving the premaxilla a steep profile, and they were longer than wide, opening slightly forward rather than straight up.
The skull featured prominent, teardrop-shaped supratemporal openings, and adults possessed four premaxillary teeth, with a minimum of 16 teeth likely present in the lower jaw.
The tibia of this animal differed from modern crocodiles by being flattened front-to-back and having a shaft that became more square further from the hip.
Fossil evidence suggests it was a semi-aquatic generalist with a broad, platyrostral skull, similar to the species Baru wickeni.
The genus was described in 2016 based on a holotype specimen found at the Low Lion Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area, though fossils are also known from the White Hunter Site.

The holotype skull of the species previously known as Baru huberi measures approximately 20 cm in length and 11 cm in width, while the fossil material used to establish the genus measured 16 to 18 cm wide between the quadrates and approximately 35 cm in length.

During the Late Oligocene, the Low Lion Site was covered by open forests lacking extensive river systems or wetlands, so the animal likely inhabited forest lakes and ponds drained by karstic limestone.
Stein et al. (2016) classified Ultrastenos as a mekosuchine crocodilian and a sister taxon to Trilophosuchus rackhami, with the parent group being Mekosuchinae.

Rio and Mannion published a study in 2021 discussing the phylogenetic position of Ultrastenos, while Lee and Yates (2018) recovered "Baru" huberi as closely related to the Bullock Creek taxon, and Ristevski et al. (2023) found a clade linking "Baru" huberi and dwarf mekosuchines, excluding Quinkana.
The type species of the genus is Ultrastenos willisi, but due to priority rules, the valid species name is Ultrastenos huberi, honoring Professor Huber.
Ultrastenos lived during the Chattian stage, from 27.3 to 23.04 million years ago.

It is debated whether Ultrastenos had a slender snout; Stein and colleagues initially proposed that it was a longirostrine animal with jaws long and narrow like modern gharials, but later studies suggest the initial interpretation of a narrow mandible was a misinterpretation and the animal actually had a more generalized lower jaw.

Willis previously considered Ultrastenos and Baru to be the same genus, using skull features to distinguish between them, yet research suggests that the fossils of Ultrastenos and the previously named species Baru huberi belong to the same animal.

It is debated whether certain cranial fossils belong to Ultrastenos or to the species Baru wickeni, with some researchers proposing they belong to a juvenile Baru wickeni, leading to suggestions that a re-description of the taxon was necessary following the discovery of related forms.

It is hypothesized that the development of slender jaws in mekosuchines may have been prevented by developmental constraints similar to those in alligators, and some researchers suggest that Harpacochampsa may be a gavialoid, which affects the phylogenetic placement of related taxa.
It is debated whether the fossils at the White Hunter Site were transported after death (thanatocoenosis) or represent true sympatry.
